subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage:
“Jatin, give it back. She was playing with that.”
“But it's my truck, Mummy!”
Elizabeth's lower lip pushed out. Her eyebrows pulled down hard and she scowled at the truck in her brother's hands. Then she lifted both arms towards Mummy.
“Oh, you look cross,” Mummy said, picking her up. “You're frustrated. Jatin took the truck.”
“She's just being dramatic,” said Jatin.
“No, she's telling us how she feels. Can she have a turn after you?”
Jatin sighed. “Two minutes.”

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do with her arms after scowling at the truck?
qa.a: She lifted both arms towards Mummy.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she pouted and scowled?
qa.a: She was most likely frustrated that the truck was taken; lifting her arms suggests she also wanted comfort, not that she was putting on a show.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Elizabeth with the big feeling?
qa.a: Mummy picked her up and named the feeling, "You're frustrated," which gives Elizabeth a word for it, then arranged a turn.

qa.q: How does Jatin see Elizabeth's pout at first?
qa.a: Jatin thinks she is being dramatic, until Mummy explains the pout is her way of showing how she feels.

grounding: It shows a toddler scowling and pouting when a toy is taken, signalling frustration and a wish for comfort, and a parent naming the feeling.

subtype: Grimace and wince at pain or taste [Expressing]
passage:
Rain drummed on the tin roof of Lalremsiami's small shop in the hill town. Her neighbour's son Dhruv was toddling between the rice sacks when he bumped his head on the counter.
He winced, squeezed his face tight and pressed a hand to his forehead.
“He's putting on a show,” a customer said.
Lalremsiami knelt, moved his hand gently and looked. A small red mark, no cut, no lump. She held a cool cloth there and watched him. Soon he was reaching for the sacks again.

qa.q: What did Dhruv bump his head on?
qa.a: He bumped his head on the counter.

qa.q: What does Dhruv's wince and tight face suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests a quick flash of pain and discomfort from the bump, a mostly reflex reaction, rather than a show; he may also have been startled.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami checked his forehead for a cut or lump and watched him afterwards, which treated the wince as a real signal of possible injury.

qa.q: What would change if Lalremsiami had agreed with the customer?
qa.a: She might have missed a real injury, and Dhruv would have been left alone with the pain.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler wincing after a bump and an adult checking for real injury instead of assuming a show or tantrum.

passage:
I'm Thomas from the ground floor. Yesterday a goat wandered into our colony car park, and little Avni from upstairs was out with her father.
She stopped dead. Mouth wide open, eyes on the goat, not a sound. I honestly couldn't tell if she was about to laugh or scream.
Then she turned and looked up at her father. He smiled, easy, and said, “Goat! Baa!”
Avni looked back at the goat, pointed, and giggled. She wanted to follow it all the way to the gate.

qa.q: Where did the goat wander in?
qa.a: It wandered into the colony car park.

qa.q: What was Avni likely feeling with her mouth wide open, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: She was most likely surprised and full of wonder at a new animal, though it could have been the start of fear; she checked her father's face to decide.

qa.q: How could a caregiver help a toddler in a moment like this?
qa.a: Stay calm, smile and name the thing, as Avni's father did, so the child can read the adult's face and feel safe.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Avni's open-mouthed stare?
qa.a: Thomas couldn't tell whether she would laugh or scream until she looked at her father and then giggled.

grounding: It shows a toddler staring open-mouthed at a new animal, which could be wonder or fear, and a caregiver's calm face helping her decide.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. From Rafiq, room lead.
Mridul had a lovely morning. When I came into the room with the snack tray, he dropped his blocks and beamed at me, his whole face crinkled, arms flapping 🙂.
At pickup he did the same for his Dadi, then hid his face in her shoulder and peeped out, still grinning.
A new helper asked if he was “buttering us up.” I said no, that's simply him being glad to see people he knows.
I smiled back each time and told his Dadi about it.

qa.q: What did Mridul drop when Rafiq came in with the snack tray?
qa.a: He dropped his blocks.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he beamed at Rafiq and his Dadi?
qa.a: He was feeling happy and delighted to see familiar people; the crinkled face and flapping arms show joy and closeness, not a plan.

qa.q: How could the new helper respond to Mridul's beaming next time?
qa.a: The helper could simply smile back and talk to him, treating the beam as a warm hello rather than a trick.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul's Dadi to get that beam at pickup?
qa.a: She probably feels loved and reassured that he is attached to her, and hearing about his morning adds to that.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler beaming at familiar caregivers out of delight and attachment, not to hide or plan anything.

passage:
Naveen unlocked the door of the flat, bag still on his shoulder, traffic horns fading behind him. Aditi was in her high chair, mashing rice with her fist.
She saw him and her whole mouth opened into a huge smile.
Naveen grinned back. “Hello, you!”
She smiled again, kicked her legs, made a gurgle.
He leaned closer and smiled, and waited. She smiled, and waited too.
They kept it up, smile for smile, until her rice was cold.

qa.q: What was Aditi doing in her high chair when Naveen came in?
qa.a: She was mashing rice with her fist.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she gave Naveen a huge open-mouthed smile?
qa.a: She seems pleased and happy to see a familiar face, and her kicking legs show excitement too.

qa.q: Why was Naveen's response a good one?
qa.a: By smiling back and waiting for her turn, he started a little back-and-forth conversation that builds their connection.

qa.q: What would change if Naveen had walked past to his phone?
qa.a: Aditi's smile would get no answer, and the playful back-and-forth would not happen.

grounding: It shows a young child giving a broad smile to a familiar face and a parent smiling back, starting an early conversation of attention.

subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]
passage:
In the courtyard of their village house, Kamal Mama held his dupatta over his face. “Where's Tanuja?” He dropped it. “There she is!”
Tanuja gave a quick flash of a smile, then looked at a hen.
“She's bored of you,” laughed his friend on the step.
But when Kamal set her on his knee and bounced her, “Horse ride, horse ride!”, Tanuja's smile stayed and stayed. She squealed for more.
“Not bored,” said Kamal. “The peekaboo smile is just quick.”

qa.q: What did Kamal Mama hold over his face for peekaboo?
qa.a: He held his dupatta over his face.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling during peekaboo, even though her smile was quick?
qa.a: She felt a quick burst of surprise and joy; the short smile fading as she looked at the hen does not mean she was bored, as the horse ride shows.

qa.q: How could Kamal's friend read short smiles better next time?
qa.a: The friend could watch across more than one game and remember that a quick smile at a surprise is normal, not a sign of disinterest.

qa.q: How does Kamal's friend see Tanuja's quick smile?
qa.a: The friend reads it as boredom and laughs about it, until the horse ride shows otherwise.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler's fleeting smile at peekaboo and sustained smile in a favourite game, with short smiles being normal.

subtype: Brow raise in surprise and attention [Expressing]
passage:
Monday. The pressure cooker whistled. Imran froze on the kitchen floor, both eyebrows shooting up, mouth round.
Thursday. The whistle again. Up went his eyebrows, but this time he looked at Damini, who looks after him while his parents are at work. “Whistle!” she said, raising her own brows back at him.
The next Monday, Imran heard the lid rattle. His eyebrows rose before the whistle even came, and when it blew, he giggled and pointed at the cooker.

qa.q: What made Imran's eyebrows shoot up on Monday?
qa.a: The pressure cooker whistled.

qa.q: What does Imran's brow raise suggest he was feeling on the first Monday?
qa.a: It suggests surprise at a sudden sound, possibly with a little alarm since he froze; by the next Monday the same raise comes with interest and amusement.

qa.q: How did Damini help Imran with the whistle?
qa.a: She named the sound and raised her own brows back in a playful way, turning the surprise into a shared game.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Imran giggles and points at the cooker?
qa.a: She would probably feel pleased and amused that the startling noise has become something funny for him.

grounding: It shows a toddler raising both eyebrows at a sudden funny sound, a fairly universal and reflexive sign of surprise and interest.

subtype: Furrowed brow in effort or upset [Expressing]
passage:
Snow fell past the window of the flat in Oslo. Ingrid sat on the rug, stacking coloured cups, a deep crease between her brows.
Her mother Clara glanced over. The frown looked almost cross. But the tower was leaning.
Clara crouched beside her. “Tricky one? Want me to hold the bottom?”
Ingrid pushed the next cup on. The crease stayed until it balanced, then smoothed out. She clapped.
When the tower fell a minute later, the brow creased again and her lip wobbled. Clara held out her arms.

qa.q: What was Ingrid stacking on the rug?
qa.a: She was stacking coloured cups.

qa.q: What did the crease between Ingrid's brows most likely mean while she stacked?
qa.a: It most likely meant effort and concentration on a leaning tower; when the tower fell, the same furrow showed she was upset and near tears.

qa.q: What did Clara do that a wise parent would copy?
qa.a: She checked the situation and offered help instead of deciding Ingrid was cross, then offered comfort when the tower fell.

qa.q: How did Clara first read Ingrid's frown?
qa.a: Clara thought it looked almost cross, until she noticed the tower was leaning.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler furrowing her brow while concentrating and before crying, and an adult checking the situation instead of assuming anger.

passage:
Bang! Crackers lit up the colony sky. Minakshi squeezed her eyes shut and pushed her face into Amma's neck.
“Minakshi, look, sparklers!” said Avni didi. “Why won't she look? She's being stubborn.”
“Not stubborn,” said Amma. “The bangs are loud. She's scared, so she's shutting them out.”
Later, on the sofa, Minakshi's eyes blinked slowly, open, shut, open.
“Now she's ignoring me,” said Avni.
Amma laughed softly. “Those are sleepy blinks. Time for bed.”

qa.q: Where did Minakshi push her face when the crackers went off?
qa.a: She pushed her face into Amma's neck.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi squeeze her eyes shut during the crackers?
qa.a: She was most likely scared of the loud bangs and shutting them out to feel safe; it was protection, not stubbornness.

qa.q: How could Avni help Minakshi next time there are crackers?
qa.a: Avni could let her stay close to Amma and show the sparklers from further away or once the bangs stop, instead of pushing her to look.

qa.q: How does Avni read Minakshi's closed eyes and slow blinks?
qa.a: Avni reads them as stubbornness and ignoring her, while Amma sees fear and then sleepiness.

grounding: It shows a toddler squeezing her eyes shut when scared and blinking slowly when sleepy, which are protective or tired signals, not defiance.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage:
The fountain in the middle of the shopping arcade was quiet. Then, with a hiss, it shot water high into the air.
Irawati went completely still in her pram. Her eyes stretched wide. Was she about to cry?
She twisted round to find her Amma's face.
Kavitha smiled and said, “Water! Whoosh!” and pointed up.
Irawati looked back at the fountain. Her shoulders loosened and she leaned forward, kicking her feet, watching every splash.

qa.q: Where was the fountain?
qa.a: It was in the middle of the shopping arcade.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when her eyes went wide, and how did she decide?
qa.a: She was startled and could have been either fascinated or alarmed; she checked her Amma's face, and the calm smile helped her settle into curiosity.

qa.q: Why was Kavitha's reaction helpful?
qa.a: Her calm smile and simple words showed Irawati the fountain was safe and fun, so the wide-eyed moment turned into wonder.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had gasped or looked worried?
qa.a: Irawati might have read the fountain as frightening and cried instead of leaning in to watch.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler widening her eyes at something new and looking to her caregiver to decide whether it is wonder or alarm.
